post_content: After a rather uneventful day at the office, I met up with the usual crowd for the EAA 690 meeting. The weather was looking a little rough as we were eating at the Flying Machine, but it was all talk and no action. After dinner, however, the action started. The radio was reporting tornado warnings for the area. We never saw one, but there was plenty of hail. Never a good thing on an airport!
Not much to report. Just a relaxing weekend with the parents. There were a few more people than usual at church today, being Easter Sunday.
For some reason, Leon Trotsky decided to ask some fairly difficult questions. Needless to say we didn’t do too well. Otherwise, it was an overall good day.
In yet another attempt to get work done, I decided to try working “remotely” today. Except for a couple interruptions, the plan mostly worked. It’ll be nice to this on a regular basis.

Ian, my personal trainer, had quite the workout for me today. I no doubt will be sore after this one. Maybe someday I’ll be able to remember the names of all the exercises so I can note what they are. Maybe...
As is often the case, I got to work late doing yet another code deployment of the software I work on. Not much else happening, thankfully.

It was a beautiful day for flying. So that is what I did. 1.4 hours logged. Up next, a simulated checkride. Sean, my instructor, and I are going to head up to Chattanooga where the checkride will take place so that I can get a sense of what to expect. Should be quite the learning experience.

post_title: Another, Not So Great, Night at Trivia
post_content: My parents and I faired our usual fair at Pizza Cafe trivia. Work is getting better and the days are longer and warmer. So all in all, everything’s going well at the moment.

Being the resident geek in my family, I get all the “technical” questions. Especially those regarding computers. My sister’s blog site is having some technical difficulties... so I’m spending a little time trying to correct them. The office work is much better at the moment. Pretty much just writing test scripts to verify my code is working as it should be.

I finally managed to convince my girlfriend to come visit me. She has a friend who’s B’day is tomorrow, so she brought her along for company... it turns out to be a great idea. They arrived around lunch, then we did some shopping downtown. Afterwards, we went flying in N1576C. I had never flown a G1000 172R before. It is very different. The girls hadn’t ever been flying with me, so it was a first for them as well. I think Charlotte has some experience in small planes, but I’m not sure Tina (her friend) did. I know they both took a lot of pictures, and hopefully they’ll send me some of them so I can post them here. Then to cap off the evening, we all went to see the Stone Mountain Laser Show. I don’t either of them had seen it. A fairly packed day that I would not have traded for anything!

Not much of interest happening. Trivia was the same... “4th place” as usual. (There is no score for less than 3rd ;-) ) Thankfully work is slowing down. I missed my workout today due to a pulled rib muscle. At least, I think that is what it is. I hope don’t have to go to doctor because of it. We’ll see...

After having been out of the gym for a week (rib injury), I went back to the personal trainer today for a “light” workout. Just so I don’t get too far out of shape. I think I’m recovering, and should be back to normal in the not-too-distant future.

The EAA invited the 2 flight schools on the field at KLZU over for the Sat. pancake breakfast. The public was also invited to come out above and beyond the usual invitation. A few did. I think everyone had a good time, and got to see a few really neat airplanes. My cross country had to be postponed due to thunderstorms in the KCHA area, but I managed to get a couple ground school hours in, and have rescheduled the flight for Wed. Hopefully the rain won’t rear its head that day.

Just another day at the office... but at trivia we won 2nd place! The questions seemed easier, and they must have been as most of the teams had high scores. My brother decided to join us again after about a 1 1/2 year hiatus. Maybe we are at the start of a winning streak...

I took the day off to get some stuff done at the airport. The weather was not good enough to fly, so Sean and I spent a couple hours in the classroom going over weather from the Oral Exam Guide. There is a lot of stuff you have to know to be a pilot! Later in the evening I went back to the Flight School for the free ground school class they have, now taught by Ernie. He Had made up a test covering airspace and charts. I think I did ok, given that half of the time I spent on the phone with my boss fixing issues at the office.

This week is my week at the airport... oddly, no flying, though. Tonight was a special FAA meeting consisting of some of the TRACON and Atlanta Center personal talking about what it is like at their facilities so we as pilots can be better informed as to what they see. Very interesting stuff, especially the IFR information. Someday it’ll all mean something to me ;-)
Paul Shirley (USAF, retired) gave a talk at the EAA 690 Hangar tonight regarding his support of Air Force 1 throughout his years of service. Lots of neat stories (at the ones he can tell).

He finally did it. David Newton is no longer a student. We’ll have to see how long it stays that way. Today he received his Master’s in Public Health (MPH) from UGA. Being a GaTech grad, I had to heckle just a little. I think the “MPH” actually stands for the speed at which you have to drive through campus so the administration can throw the diploma in the window :-)

Another trivia under our belt.. but not another win. We just can’t seem to compete with the larger teams. Maybe someday Mr. Leon Trotsky will ask a few questions that we know and the know-it-alls do not. Someday....

Ian, my personal trainer, is taking the weekend off to go on vacation. At least, that is what his wife has told him. So, today was my last workout for a week. I hope I’m still about to do a workout when he gets back.

Today’s ground school was a test about weather. There were quite a few questions that I did not know. Thankfully it was an open book test. The only problem was, which book to use to find the information being asked.

As usual, the office has me rather busy. I’m trying to get ready for being in the woods for a few days, without phone or internet access. I don’t know how the office is going to cope, but they have no choice.

Roger, his sister Carrie, and I drove up to Vogel State Park in Blairsville, GA today to start a 12+ mile hike through the north Georgia mountains. It should prove to be a fun trip, and I know we will not go hungry. I think we brought enough food for a couple weeks.

In reading over the guide book about the Coosa Trail, it states that parts of the trail are “moist”. Given that it rained all day, I think the whole trail has come to be known as “moist”. At least by the three of us. Also, if Escher ever designed a trail, I think it was this one. It just keeps going up and up and up.

Well, the trail continued to go up, but it did eventually start going down, and we managed to get back to the back country office just as they were closing. What a weekend. I think the plan for next weekend is doing absolutely nothing.
Back in the office, thankfully. I need a vacation from the vacation :-) Tomorrow I expect to have a lot of visitors, so I’m resting up while I can.

Simon and Mostafa from AmDocs arrived today, and we started going over all the things necessary to do the software upgrade we are about to do next month. Lots of work to be done, I just hope we have enough time to do it.

Tonight’s ground school was about cross country planning. There were 3 of of in the class (4 teachers) and I think I must know my stuff. I managed to get the flight plan completed in under half the time of the others, and got it all correct. I just hope I do as well on the check ride.

My personal trainer got a new toy and waited for me to try it out. It is a weight vest capable of holding 100 lbs of bean-bag like weights. We did today’s workout with 20 lbs, and I was very happy to take off the vest when we were done. It sure makes the workout harder.

It is time, once again, to do a little cleaning at the front of the neighborhood. About 5 or 6 of us managed to attend for a little weed pulling, trimming, and laying of pine needles. It looks a lot better now. Eventually we’ll buy some trees for the other side of the entrance, but first we need to do some stump grinding. All in due time... as for the rest of the day, it was spent with Roger playing Mario Cart. We said we were going to take it easy, and we did!

With most of the normal church staff on vacation, we were done to the bare bones for today’s service. Still it went fairly well. I’d have to say that Steve Vrooman’s best talent is not public speaking, but all-in-all he did a good job. Now about that evolution theory non-sense. I can see how there are those that believe in creationism, but to state that evolution is not right, is preposterous.

Memorial Day is a well timed holiday. After several months of no holidays, it is very much welcomed. I happened to take advantage of the day by cleaning up my pond. Which needed cleaning very badly. Now it is much, much better, but still needs a little attention. Hopefully I can keep it about where it is now, or better.

I suppose a few students have been doing their check rides recently. The instructors at the flight school seem to be taking notes during the oral part of the test and sharing them with the rest of us students. Thank you! Any little bit of help is greatly appreciated.

And now for something completely different. I managed to catch a ride with a fellow flight school student down to Falcon Field in Peachtree City, GA for a tour of the Atlanta Terminal Radar Approach Control (TRACON) facility. What an experience! Even if you are not a pilot, if you ever get a chance to take a tour, DO SO!

After getting a small taste of flying (granted from the back seat) yesterday, I just had to go flying today. So I arranged a quick 1.2 hour local flight with Sean. I was quite a bit rusty from being away nearly 2 months, but started to get back into it. Boy do I need to work on cross wind landings.

Tonight a group of people decided to have a birthday party at the Pizza Cafe. All I can say is “bad timing”. Don’t they know that the Pizza Cafe is an extremely busy place on Monday nights? Oh well, I think everyone that wanted to be there managed to find a place. Let’s hope this doesn’t become a trend.

This evening’s ground school covered several different subjects. A few weeks back, I requested the topic of weather. Apparently this one has Ernie a little stumped as he seems to be taking the subject is stages. I don’t blame him. It is quite a complicated subject. I think he is doing a lot of research to try and make the most of it.

For the past few days, I've been battling against mother nature in the back yard.  The war is not over, but I feel we've reached a truce... for now. I did it!  I finally Passed!  For those who want to know the details, here is a re-cap of the day's events.

4:00 AM - Wake up.  I can't sleep, too much going on in my head... most of it aviation related.  For the next few hours I'm going over all the paperwork and getting ready for the day.

6:30 AM - At the airport.  A little early, yes, but I didn't know what Atlanta traffic would do and I wasn't going to be late for anything!  Needless to say, I sat in the car reading more about weather and the FARs.

7:00 AM - Ernie drives up, and we begin the pre-flight of the airplane.  The temperature was 4C and the dew point was also 4C, and the plane had a thin layer of ice covering the top of the wings and the windshield.  I must have used 1/2 of the spray bottle (alcohol) de-icing the wings.  The windshield was the hard one.  I didn't know what effect the alcohol would have on the windshield, so I sprayed a light layer on it, then using a bucket of water, washed it off.  I think the only way the ice ever got off that windshield was due to the heat in my hands... boy was that cold!

8:40 AM - Yesterday, I had signed up with FlightAware.  And thus when Ernie and I filed our flight plan (IFR), I got the following email:

From: FlightAware Alerts <alerts@flightaware.com>

Subject: N5355F filed a flight plan KLZU -> KCHA

Date: October 20, 2009 8:40:33 AM EDT

To: Brian Stephen Michael <bsmichae42@yahoo.com>

N5355F has just filed a flight plan.  A C72R is scheduled to depart from KLZU (Gwinnett County) at 08:45AM EDT heading for KCHA (Lovell Field) for an estimated arrival at 09:45AM EDT.

Expected route: NOONE V97 NELLO

For more information visit http://flightaware.com/live/flight/N5355F

9:19 AM - Then when we finally managed to get into the air, another email.  The flight was for the most part, uneventful.  Calm winds, little to no clouds, and almost no traffic.  I couldn't have asked for better conditions.  At one point, we did have the radio go out on us.  It probably was only for about a minute, but when flying IFR, having the radio fail is a BAD thing.  Thankfully it started working again, but I don't think it was the result of anything Ernie or I did.  A sign of things to come...

From: FlightAware Alerts <alerts@flightaware.com>

Subject: N5355F has departed KLZU for KCHA

Date: October 20, 2009 9:19:26 AM EDT

To: Brian Stephen Michael <bsmichae42@yahoo.com>

N5355F has departed KLZU (Gwinnett County) enroute to KCHA (Lovell Field) for an estimated arrival at 10:14AM EDT

For more information visit http://flightaware.com/live/flight/N5355F

10:20 AM - We arrive in the KCHA (Chattanooga) area, and can see the evidence for the IFR weather forecast we received.  The mountains to the northwest and southeast formed a bowl that managed to hold in a 500 foot think layer of clouds just over the airport.  We heard a pilot report stating that he had broken out about 900 feet MSL.  The field elevation is 683 feet MSL, and Ernie looked at me and said there was no way the ceiling was that high.  As we aligned ourselves with the runway, Ernie took the controls and we began our decent into the clouds.  But, just before entering the clouds, Ernie noticed that the NAV1 radio was out, the needle on the VOR indicator was not functional and our glide slope indicator was also not functional.  Ernie proceeded to do a go-around, and contacted the tower, letting them know of our equipment failure, also asking if an ASR approach was available.  The tower responded that an ASR approach was available, and began giving us vectors for another approach.  I could tell Ernie had been through this before, as he didn't hesitate a bit, and managed to have me help him out where I could.  Then I get my final FlightAware email for the trip:

From: FlightAware Alerts <alerts@flightaware.com>

Subject: N5355F arrived at KCHA from KLZU

Date: October 20, 2009 10:26:53 AM EDT

To: Brian Stephen Michael <bsmichae42@yahoo.com>

N5355F arrived at KCHA (Lovell Field) at 10:05AM EDT from KLZU (Gwinnett County)

For more information visit http://flightaware.com/live/flight/N5355F

10:30 AM - We walk into TAC Air South and see Ben sitting in the lobby, on the phone with another prospective checkride client.  The place was under a complete renovation due to all the rain we had been having over the preceding month.  Apparently, a gutter had broken over the building, and flooded the entire place.  Build inspectors had found mold in the walls, so the whole place was getting an overhaul.  Ben told us that he hadn't had an office in weeks.  All the construction made for a little more difficulty in getting the paperwork out of the way, and thankfully Ben had a cell phone card for his laptop to use for interacting with the FAA.  He was very happy to hear that I had managed to get all the IACRA paperwork done online, as he really didn't have a way to do everything the "old" way. He quickly went over what the agenda was to be, and asked if I was ready.  I was, so off we go.

10:50 AM - Oral begins.  Ben had everything as hand written notes, and we pretty much just went down the list.  I happened to have a similar list of notes from a previous checkride he had given.  That was immensely helpful.  Also, he seemed to want to get it done as quick as possible, so he talked through everything as quick as he could, to which I answered as quickly as I could.  Naturally, I made a mistake or two, but overall no real issues.  Here is a breakdown of the questions asked: (* indicates areas where I hesitated.  It is, afterall, a test :-) ).

  • Carry passenger requirements
  • Personal documents
  • Medical class requirements
  • Airplane documents
  • AD's
  • Class C radio equipment
  • ELTs
  • Maintenance requirements
  • Inoperative equipment, procedures
  • What is a ferry permit?  How do you get one?
  • VSI needle stuck, what to do?
  • Show your example cross country flight log from KCHA to KSAV
  • Fuel reserves
  • Cruising altitudes
  • Fuel burn and time
  • Sectional chart, runway lights, beacon, field elevation, radio frequencies, what is the CTAF for?
  • Victor airways, military airways * (I had to think for a moment on this one), west vs. east headings and their appropriate altitude
  • Bravo airspace, what ATC requirements are their to enter?
  • What and where is class A airspace?
  • Show example of class D on sectional
  • Know the various heights of class E, especially around class G airports
  • Legally go through a restricted area?
  • What is the white line around Atlanta on sectional? (Terminal Area Chart)
  • Weight and balance.  How to check within limits?  What does the area to the right on the center of gravity moment envelope mean in terms of tail heavy vs. nose heavy? *
  • Aft center of gravity hazards?  (less stable)
  • Is the airplane approved for spins? (yes in utility category). *  (originally, I answered no.  He was lenient with me and explained that the answer was yes, in the utility category)
  • How to recover from a spin? (opposite rudder, lower pitch)
  • Wake turbulence.  How do you land after a heavy jet?
  • Take off distance.  Show how you get it.
  • How do you get pressure altitude?
  • Hotter air, how does it affect take off distance?
  • How does lower pressure affect take off distance?
  • Fuel burn, amount per hour.  How to lean the engine?
  • Oil minimum, maximum and grade for the plane you will be using for the practical part of the test?
  • Fuel required for your plane (100 octane low lead) and it color (blue).
  • Pitot tube blocked, what instruments are affected?
  • Static blocked, what instruments are affected?
  • What is Vx?  (Best angle of climb)  What is that speed for your airplane?
  • What is Vy? (Best rate of climb)  What is that speed for your airplane?
  • Can Va change?  What does Va do with lower than max gross weight?
  • Vacuum pump fails, what gauge shows it?  What instruments are affected?
  • Alternater fails, what happens to instruments?
  • What stops working when the battery is drained?
  • What is the source of cabin heat?  What is dangerous about it? (carbon monoxide)
  • What can happen physiologically at high altitudes? (hypoxia)
  • Oxygen requirements are various altitudes.
  • How do you treat passengers suffering from hyperventilation?
  • Alcohol consumption.  How long to wait before flying?
  • Scuba diving.  How long to wait after getting out of the water?  (12 hours recommended; 24 hours if compression stops are involved in ascent)
  • Runway markings.  Chevrons before threshold means what?  Arrows before threshold means what?
  • What color are the runway lights at the threshold? (green)
  • Two light VASI and PAPI.  What does the various red/white light combinations mean?
  • What transponder code to use in emergency?
  • What does a flashing green light mean from a control tower?
  • Night flight.  What steps are to be taken to prepare your eyes?  Always carry flashlights, but only required for airlines.
  • How do you turn on the lights at an airport with pilot controlled lighting?
  • Narrower runways look different when approaching to land how?  (narrower makes you think you are higher)
  • What do puffy clouds tend to indicate? (unstable air)
  • Cold fronts typically have what kind of clouds?
  • Be able to read off a METAR or TAF.

12:00 PM - Oral complete.  I was so caught up in the oral, that I really didn't pay any attention to what Ernie was doing, or anyone else for that matter.  We turned around and saw Ernie chatting with a couple military guys (I think Marines, but they may have been Navy).  He saw that we were finished and said "is it lunch time yet?"  We were all ready to get a bit to eat, and I really wanted to try out this bar-be-que place that everyone raves about.  So we head over to the bar-be-que place and each of us get the pork plate.  I must say it was quite good.

1:30 PM - Practical test begins.  We start off with a preflight check.  He said to treat it as if it was the first flight of the day.  He really wasn't very scrutinizing on how I did it, but did ask the occasional question about what I was looking for, or what something was.  For example, the V shaped antenna on the empennage are the VOR antenna.  The rubber belt inside the cowling is the alternator belt (not the starter, as I answered.  I got a bit carried away :-) ).  With the pre-flight complete we get in the plane.  He tells me that I don't have to explain how the seat belt works (being nice) and that in case of an emergency he would let me handle it to the best of my ability, but would take over if he saw it was too much for me.  I guess a little self-preservation on his part.  I didn't mind.  In the same sense of humor, I let him know I needed to call out "clear prop" to start the engine, but no one would likely hear me, as there were a couple Navy jets behind us doing a run-up.  I couldn't hear a thing.

Engine started, I contact Chattanooga Clearance and let them know that I'm heading to the southeast at 5,500 feet.  I'm not too good at talking to clearance delivery at this point, as I had only done it twice before, so naturally I made a few mistakes in my call.  Ben didn't seem to think that was a problem, especially since I knew I had made mistakes immediately after making them, and corrected myself where appropriate.  After I get my clearance, I contact ground and let them know I'm ready to move.  Again, making the mistake of not telling ground where I was.  They didn't ask, so I guess they kindof knew, and gave me taxi instructions to runway 20.  While taxi'ing, Ben made sure to caution me about staying away from the new red and white line around the terminal building.  Apparently they have motion sensors around the building... boy is the TSA paranoid!  I complete the run up behind a couple Cessna Citations, and make my way to the runway.

I switch over to tower's frequency and let them know I'm ready for departure.  Ben wanted me to do a normal departure for the first one, just to get a feel for what he was in for :-).  I think I did quite well, keeping the plane in line with the runway centerline until about 700 feet AGL.  Then turned to the left as directed by my clearance, and started getting on my cross country route as I had planned a few days prior.

Once I get on my desired heading, now it is just a matter of getting up to altitude, but Ben cuts me short and states that I did fine and to abort the cross country and divert to KDNN (Dalton, GA).  He didn't want to waste our time getting up 5,500 just to descend back down for some landings at Dalton.  He then asked me to do a short field landing at Dalton.  I tuned into the AWOS station at Dalton and noted the current weather.  Then tuned into the CTAF for Dalton and didn't hear anyone else in the pattern, so I radio'ed for airport advisories.  The UNICOM operator came up and said they were landing runway 32 and that no one else was in the pattern.  I thanked him, and started a 45 entry into downwind.  The biggest issue I had was remembering to use "Dalton" and not "Winder" in my radio calls.  Oh how we get into ruts at times :-)  Ben just laughed, and said he'd experienced the same.  I did the remainder of the calls, on down wind, turning base, and turning final.  Then came in for what I think is my best short field landing yet.  He didn't want me to brake too hard, so I didn't and we turned off at the first available taxi way.

So far, no problems, so he had me setup for a short field take off.  I did, and we were off again.  This time I stayed in the pattern, doing my call outs as I'm supposed to, setting up for a soft field landing.  I was a little high on my approach, but still managed to land within 200 feet of my designated touch down point.  Again, turning onto the first available taxi way.  Back taxi'ing, Ben let me know the next take off was to be a soft field one.  I did as asked, and we performed a straight out departure of the pattern to the north.

Once we were far enough away from Dalton, he had me do a turn around a point, but cautioned me to find a point with a field nearby, as I was to expect an engine failure shortly after completing the maneuver.  If only all engine failures were as predictable as that!  I had a small problem initiating the maneuver, as I had picked out a point, but lost to point while turning the plane to do a clearing turn.  After a few moments, I found the point again, and around I went.  Just as soon as I had straightened out from the turn, he said, "ok, you just had an engine failure".  At 800 feet AGL, that is a particularly bad time to experience such a failure... but the field right next to the point (a small radio tower) was really easy to line up and land in.  Once Ben was satisfied that I could make the field, we pushed back in the throttle, and climbed back to about 3,000 feet MSL.  Then it was time for a power off stall.  I do my clearing turn, and go right into the stall.  I've done these sooo many times, it was second nature to me.  With that out of the way, he had me go into a power on stall.  Also, no problems on the power on stall.

We then contact KCHA approach and let them know we are coming back into their airspace for landing.  They are not too busy, so give us instructions to head on in to runway 20.  The landing was uneventful, and we taxi'ed back to TAC Air south.

3:00 PM - Practical test complete.  Ben logs into the FAA system and sets me up as a newly licensed pilot!

3:45 PM - Start return trip to KLZU.  Also uneventful.  We make the trip in about an hour, and chat about a few things along the way.  After all the day's flying, it was good to be back at KLZU.

4:45 PM - Back at KLZU.

Raman Divakaran took a trip up in N5355F with me on Jan. 31, 2010.  It was my first flight of the year, and Raman's first flight in a "small" airplane.  The flight was 1.5 hours total, starting at KLZU, 1 landing at KWDR, and returning back to KLZU.  For the most part at rather uneventful trip... the best kind :-)  He took a few pictures, so I've posted them on Flickr for everyone to see.  I also just received my audio cable that allows me to record the conversations/ATC audio from the flight.  If you are interested in 1 1/2 hours of audio, take a listen.

Now that I have a few tools to work with, I figured I'd try my hand at the Van's "Class Project". Essentially, it is a section of a wing that requires the use of most of the techniques in building an airplane. All I can say is I'm learning a LOT! Here is the same stiffener, but looking at it from a different direction.  Not much to look at, and you definitely wouldn't think that this is the result of about 3 hours work.  Did I mention that I'm just getting started? :-) And this is that same piece again, cleco'd to the wing skin.  I'm keeping the blue plastic coating on the skin because I know that I'll just end up scratching it the moment I take it off.

Now the project is starting to move along.  As you can see, the clecos are brass in color.  That means I'm starting to use the 1/8th (a.k.a. AN470AD4-4) thick rivets.  It is definitely neat to see pieces start to go together.  It just makes it "look" like there is some progress being made. Of course, there are always two sides to the spar, so here is a shot of the other side.  You can see the ribs under the spar.  I haven't gotten to those yet. To the right you can see the full spar with both doublers cleco'd to it.  I still have some deburring to do.  The doublers (blue square pieces) have their holes pre-drilled, which does make the process a whole lot easier. One the left I've added the ribs into the mix.  Still haven't riveted anything yet, but at least wanted to see what the thing looked like somewhat put together.  ...and I can definitely see how it is supposed to go together.  Now to figure out how to use that squeezer... Well, I figured out the squeezer.  All I can say is AN470AD4-4 rivets are hard to squeeze!  Even with the Cleaveland Tools squeezer (which is supposed to be easier to use), it was quite a challenge.  Time to do some more upper bod workouts at the gym. Looking down the other side of the project thus far.  Looking good ;-)

Jonathan and I go on a camping trip about every other year.  This year we were trying to go to Canada, but the logistics were just too much. He came up with the idea of Saranac Lake, and it turned out to be a good one.  We got his truck all packed up, then headed over to his church for a quick softball game. Our first night was in Lee, MA, which was just a few hours down the road.  Since the church is actually east of Worcester, it took a little longer to get to Lee than it would have if we'd left directly from Jonathan's house, but it was a game he wasn't willing to miss. Once we got to the lakes, we "put in" on Lower Saranac Lake.  Between the Lower Saranac and Middle Saranac there is a lock.  This is the first time I've ever been through a lock, much less a self service one.  On the right is the view from the lower lake. Naturally, while we were there, we had to get out and look around.  The instructions for operating the lock were pretty straight forward.  We also we lucky in that a ranger was there, and he actually did most of the work for us. I made sure to get several shots of the whole thing.  It is really quite elegant in it's simplicity.  Gravity runs the thing.  The doors on the lower side (right) are held closed by the pressure from the water of the middle lake. At least when the doors from the middle lake are open.  As long as one set of doors are closed at all times, all is well.  There is a overrun not too far off, so the lake level shouldn't get so high as to over take the locks. Once we got to our camping spot we did a little setting up, found a perch up on some rocks, sat back, and watched the sun set and moon rise. Our camp site was on an island, so we weren't too concerned about bears.  There were, however, a few squirrels, so we did have to keep our stuff somewhat secured.  Jonathan and I did the REI freeze dried approach to food.  I think we'll try more of a mix of things in the future.  And let me just say that the freeze dried biscuits and gravy... well, I don't think we'll be doing that one again ;-). The trail leading up to the camp site came down to the area seen on the right.  Getting out of a canoe here is not exactly easy, but it was doable.  The rocks did provide a convenient location to rest the canoe.

It has been awhile.  Work and other things get in the way.  That's something I'm going to have to figure out when it comes to doing the real thing.  I'll never finish the plane if I go at this rate. At this point I've riveted a large number of the AN426AD3-3 rivets that hold the skin on to the spar and ribs.  Since I'm not going to prime this project, it is fairly difficult to get a picture of the inside, but here are a couple attempts.  To the right you should be able to see where the bucking bar slipped a little while driving the rivet with my 3x gun.  I'm still new to this, and all I can do is hope I get a lot better. Hopefully at least one of these is good enough to be able to see how things look on the inside.  The outside is definitely easier to get a picture of. Looking at the outside, you can see the left is cleco'd and the right is mostly riveted.  The instructions (under the workpiece) state that the rivets near the top of the workpiece will require either a special bucking bar, or a special squeezer yoke.  Personally, I'm leaning towards the special yoke. Just for the sake of doing it, I took another shot from the other side.  Going forward, I may not take as many pictures... but we'll see. On the right, I've removed the clecos and let the skin open up a little.  It is a bit easier to see down the inside, but it is still pretty shinny down in there.

The Thursday night "ground school" gang (including myself) wanted to go on a trip, now that we are all licensed private pilots.  Dave has his own plane, which left Mike and I to rent one from The Flight School.  We ended up taking N7262X.  Come to find out, the power connector in 62X is a special connector, not the typical cigarette lighter.  So our plans of using Mike's aera were dashed.  We did get to use it a little, as it had at least an hour's worth of battery. And it is a good thing we had it.  The weather wasn't completely perfect.  Thunderstorms in the area around Gulf Shores due to a tropical storm that was nearby.  However, most of the flight was pretty nice weather wise.  Mike wanted to see how high we could get. On the ground at KLZU, the reported weather was 3,500 feet density altitude, so I wasn't expecting to get too high. By the time we got south of Atlanta, we were coming up on 10,500 feet.  At this point, we could have spun the plane and had lots of time to recover. As proof of the altitude we got to, I made sure to snap a picture of the panel showing us at nearly full throttle and just a little above 10,500.  The clouds made the trip a little more eventful, as we had to do a few left and right turns to avoid them.  We're not yet instrument rated, you know. Before landing at KJKA in Gulf Shores, I took a picture of the two of us with my iPhone.  Would you go on a trip with these two? When it came time to land, I took some video of the whole thing.  It is about 15 minutes long.  You can somewhat see the stormy weather to the right and the shore to the left.  Pensacola approach was vectoring us a little to avoid the weather and their airspace.  I think we timed things just right.  IMG_0041.mov

From programmer to pilot... Life has a funny way of taking us on a wild ride, and I am no exception. Born in Lexington, KY, I've lived in nearly every state in the southeast United States. It had been a few years, and my parents wanted to take my nephews to D.C., so I tagged along.  Upon arriving, we boarded on of the double decker buses for a tour around the city.  The tour, which started at Union Station, made it's first stop at the U.S. Capital. Thankfully most of the construction that I remember from previous trips has been completed, so this time I was actually able to "see" the capital. The view from the top of the bus was actually pretty good, albeit, fairly cold. Continuing on, we head up the hill to visit the cathedral.  We didn't stop to get out, but the bus did pause for a moment or two.  Just long enough to take a few pictures.  One item of note.  When they say "stay seated", they mean stay seated.  The power lines and tree branches that cross the street are literally just above the height of the bus. The next day, we start out at the Washington Monument.  I have to say that the new way of getting people up to the top is much better than it had been.  Last I remember, the line wrapped around the monument several times, and many people wasted a great number of hours.  Now you make a reservation and show up for your allotted time slot. I decided to take a few pictures while at the top.  The view was actually quite good and the weather was extremely cooperative.  Looking down on the Lincoln Memorial, the view now includes the World War II Memorial.  I'd been to it in years past, but the view from the air definitely puts it into perspective. As you can see from the shot on the left, the White House is in the process of setting up their Christmas tree. Going to the east side, I managed to get a fairly good shot of the Mall, Smithsonian Museums, and the Capital.  For some reason I keep thinking the distance is a lot less than it actually is.  Maybe this picture will remind me ;-) Sunday night, my sister wanted me to go to one of her favorite hangouts.  First we stopped by her place to fix a few things.  Then we took the short walk over to The Mighty Pint.  On the way, we meet up with a friend of hers, Roxana.  Cute, are they not? :-) Monday morning, we head over to the Library of Congress for a few minutes so we don't have to wait outside at the capital too long (in the cold).  Come to find out, the capital has spent a few dollars, about a billion, re-doing the way visitors get into the building. Inside, not much has actually changed. The two of my nephews who were able to get out that day are featured on the right.  For the most part, they were fairly well behaved. Now we come to one of my favorite parts of the city, at least favorite amongst the touristy parts of the city, the Air and Space Museum.  This is my first time there since Space Ship One has been added to the aircraft of display.  It is hard to believe that a ship so small managed to accomplish so much. At the other end of the accomplishment spectrum is the Wright Flyer.  According to the signs in the museum, this is the original 1903 craft.  Other than the cloth covering the wings, everything is original.  I'm just impressed that it flew for as long as it did, when it did.  I'm also glad it did ;-) Ethan is apparently in a penguin phase.  Here he is with his alter-ego.  How Ethan got in the case and managed to get the penguin to kneel next to him, I'll never know :-o  Seriously though, both he and David seemed to enjoy the natural history museum, especially the dinosaurs! T-Rex and the brontosaurus (at least I think that is a brontosaurus) haven't changed much in the 20 or so years that I've been going to D.C.  This time around I noticed a few more creatures than I have in the past.  Some that I hadn't ever heard of before, like an "even".  When Kate pointed out the name, all I could say was, "that's odd"! Taking off from KDCA, the weather was just good enough to allow a couple pictures before we were up in the clouds. I wonder how long it will be before I'm back?

Hours: 2.0 Manual Ref: Page 6-4, step 5; Page 7-6, Step 13 Partner: N/A I've started the priming process! Well, at least the prep work for priming. I've opt'ed to go with the following approach:
  1. Clean the part with acetone. Using a paper towel to rub the acetone. This pretty effectively cleans off any oil, markings, etc. So be prepared to remember what part is what ;-)
  2. Scratch the part with a scotch-brite pad. I tried the "store" variety scotch-brite pads (those joined to a sponge). They just don't seem to do the trick. A "7447" scotch-brite pad does exactly what it should ;-)
  3. Spray the part with alumiprep. I'm using a generic garden sprayer from the aviation department of my local Ace Hardware.
  4. Spray the part with water, to rinse off the alumiprep. I'm using a sprayer that I bought in the aviation department of my local Lowe's
I'll fill in the rest of the steps after I do them (so I know what they are).  It looks like that may be a few days, as the temperatures are just too low to be applying primer :-(

Hours: 3.0 Manual Ref: Page 6-4, step 5; Page 7-6, Step 13 Partner: N/A The temperature got to a balmy 53 Fahrenheit today! So, I'm continuing from where I left off...
  1. Mix a few ladles of Akzo primer part A with part B in a plastic paint bucket, and get HPLV gun ready to spray.
  2. Put on a full body paint suit (you're going to need it!)
  3. Spray each part enough to completely cover with primer, but not so much that it runs.
  4. Allow parts to dry for about an hour, even though they are probably dry in about 10 to 15 minutes.
The Akzo primer actually does go on pretty nice, and I now understand why in all of my research I could not find any pictures or videos of the priming process. It is a VERY messy process. Even with a fairly elaborate paint booth, a little bit of the over spray managed to get out, but not enough to harm anything. Since I had not managed to clean the rudder skins before I started spraying primer, I still have to do those pieces, but that should be a small task.  You can see the primer "dust" on the vinyl covering that is still on the vertical stabilizer.  It truly gets on everything.

Hours: 10.0 Manual Ref: Page 6-4, Steps 6 and 7; Page 6-5, Steps 1, 2, and 3; Page 6-6, Steps 1 through 8 Partner: N/A At long last, I've driven my first rivet! I knew this was going to be a long and involved project, but just the vertical stabilizer took a huge amount of time to rivet together. Good thing I like a challenge :-).  I marked the first driven rivet head in black with a sharpie.  I have no idea if the mark will stay there, but it'll be neat to look back on when the whole thing is done.  Here are some pictures of the progress. Note: There is a step 9 on page 6-6 that I haven't yet completed.  It is to rivet rear spar caps to the rear spar below where the skin meets the spar.  I don't have a 3/32 AN470 squeezer set, and my arms are too tired to use the rivet gun at this point, so I'll have to re-visit this step when I've recovered.

Hours: 2.0 Manual Ref: Page 7-7, Steps 1 through 4 Partner: N/A After the EAA690 breakfast, I tried my hand at driving a few more rivets. My arms are still tired from yesterday :-( I did manage to make some progress. I haven't yet primed the rudder skins, which I plan on doing when I prime the first few parts of the horizontal stabilizer. That should be coming up pretty soon.

Hours: 6.0 Manual Ref: Page 8-2, Steps 1 through 4 Partner: N/A I decided to tackle the rear horizontal stabilizer spar before the next round of priming, just so I didn't have to get all suited up more times than I absolutely had to. I do not like the priming process! On a more positive note, a simple file does wonders for deburring spars :-)  I also created another time-lapse video of the deburring process, and yes, I did do this after church ;-)

Hours: 1.0 Manual Ref: Page 7-7, Step 5 Partner: N/A I had an hour before heading off to trivia, so I spent it doing a little back riveting on one of the rudder skins. No pictures, sorry :-( I'll be sure to put up a video of the rest of the process in next few days.

Hours: 8.0 Manual Ref: Page 7-8, Steps 1, 2 and 3; Page 7-9 Step 1; Page 8-2, Steps 1 through 6; Page 8-3, Steps 1 and 2 Partner: N/A Here is another time-lapse video of me back-riveting the rudder stiffeners onto the rudder skins. I managed to make some more progress on the horizontal stabilizer rear spar. Hopefully I'll be making a lot more progress over the weekend.

Hours: 1.0 Manual Ref: Page 8-3, Step 3 Partner: N/A The left front spar attachment is made from a piece of AA6-187x2x2 1/2 angle. The measurements in the plans are very precise, so I'm taking my time on this step. Pictures to be coming soon.
Hours: 2.0 Manual Ref: Page 8-3, Step 3 & 4 Partner: N/A In between other things, I managed to knock out the left and right front spar attachments. That band saw purchase was definitely worth it!
Hours: 5.5 Manual Ref: Page 8-4, Step 1; Page 8-5, Step 1 Partner: N/A Lots, and lots, and lots of deburring! Did I mention there was some deburring?

Hours: 9 Manual Ref: Page 8-5, Steps 1 through 8; Page 8-6, Steps 3 & 4; Page 8-7, Steps 1, 2, and 5 Partner: N/A With the spar deburred, it was time to move on to match drilling the spar caps and doubler. There are a lot of holes to work with. As you can see in the "Manual Ref" header, I skipped a step or two, especially the steps that say "prime if desired". I plan on coming back to those. Oh yea, and here in Atlanta, we got a little snow ;-)

Hours: 4.5 Manual Ref: Page 8-7 Partner: N/A I may have skipped a step or two, but I wanted to see how it all looks when it comes together. Now that I have a few pictures, it is time to take it back apart and keep deburring. There was a side benefit to putting it all together. The plans say to make a 9 degree bend in a few pieces. 9 degrees is pretty hard to discern, so seeing the pieces in their final positions made it very easy to see if there was too much or too little bend. All-in-all, I really don't have too much more to go on the horizontal stabilizer.

Hours: 3.5 Manual Ref: Page 8-7, Steps 1 & 3; Page 8-8, Steps 1 through 8 Partner: N/A I spent a few hours taking apart the "test fit" I had done the day before and completed the deburring work on the HS-1004 and HS-905 ribs. Then it was a simple matter of following the steps on page 8-8. Mostly it was a lot of final drilling with the #30 drill bit and cleco'ing all the parts together. I thought I had enough cleco's until I made my wings kit purchase, I was wrong. Apparently the horizontal stabilizer uses a LOT of 3/32 clecos. Needless to say, I have an order in for another 100 (along with a 3/32 cupped set for my squeezer :-) )

Hours: 5.5 Manual Ref: Page 8-9, steps 1 through 8 Partner: N/A This was a lot of cleco pulling and moving, as well as drilling! There truly are a lot of holes in the horizontal stabilizer. This is also the first time I'm using the right-angle drill that I picked up from Harbor Freight. It works pretty well, but I probably should have practiced a little more on scrap pieces than I did. Thankfully, I didn't scratch the stringer web (HS-1016) too much. After doing a little reading of other builder's logs, I think I want to spend a little more time deburring all these parts. Just to be safe. I don't want to end up with any cracks because I was going too fast and didn't properly debur something during the build process ;-)

Hours: 1 Manual Ref: Page 9-2, steps 1 & 7 Partner: N/A Now that the horizontal stabilizer is final drilled and taken apart in preparation for priming, it is time to start getting the elevators ready for the same. I had put a wood cutting band in the band saw to help out my personal trainer, so it took me a little time to get the band switched back, but I did manage to spend about an hour cutting apart the various rib pieces.

The Thursday Night Gang made an attempt to visit First Flight Field (KFFA) where the Wright Brothers did their flying a little over 100 years ago. Apparently it is easier to get there on the ground than by air. We didn't quite make it to the field, but we got really, really close. It was excellent IFR training experience, though. Hours: 2 Manual Ref: Page 9-2, steps 1 Partner: N/A Just keeping everyone informed, and the time totals up-to-date... I've had a bit of buildus interruptus of the past week or two. Just the usual suspects (work, other projects, trip to KFFA, etc.) No pictures, as there really isn't much to see. I am still adding to the pile of aluminum shavings on the garage floor, so don't be too concerned.

Hours: 2 Manual Ref: Page 9-2, steps 1 Partner: N/A Have I mentioned that there is some deburring of metal involved in building an airplane? Well, another 2 hours spent whittling away at the spars and ribs of the elevators. Just lots of tedious work.

Hours: 5 Manual Ref: Various steps on Pages 9-8, 9-9, and 9-10 Partner: Chase Michael For a couple hours in the morning I managed to finish getting the spars and ribs of the elevators deburred.  Later in the day, my youngest nephew, Chase, wanted to check out how the plane was coming along.  While he was there, I had him help me out with a few steps.  Naturally, the order in the plans wasn't exactly followed, but he certainly enjoyed putting the pieces together.  In the picture where the right elevator is pictured with him between the workbenches, he managed to place all the clecos pictured.  Not bad for a 6 year old!

Hours: 4.5 Manual Ref: Pages 9-4, 9-5, 9-6, and 9-7 up to step #2 Partner: N/A Since I skipped a few steps with my nephew a couple days ago, I had to go back and actually do the steps properly.  It was nice to see how all the pieces go together, though.  Basically it was a lot of drilling and cleco'ing.  You can see me in the first picture, taking the picture with my iPhone.  I don't have too many with me in the reflection.  I guess now you can see how I'm taking all these pictures.  If you pay close attention, you can see where I've cleco'd the elevator trim access doubler to... nothing! (the picture with the white label of E-615PP)

Hours: 2 Manual Ref: Page 9-7 Step #3 Partner: N/A No pictures, but did want to make an entry for the couple hours spent final drilling the skins of 1 of the elevators with the underlying framework.  Still have the other elevator to do.

Hours: 3.5 Manual Ref: Page 9-7 steps 3 through 7 Partner: N/A After a couple hours final drilling LOTS of holes in the elevator skins, it came time to drill the holes as marked in the plans for the trim cable anchor brackets. I figured I'd use my drill press, but even in the press, the drill bit tended to migrate. Even with the work pieces clamped to the drill press table. The bit actually wanted to bend. Oh well... the holes are still acceptable distances from the edges and now they are fairly easy to figure out which goes where when I reassemble them after priming. I know others are re-enforcing the welds that Vans does for this piece. Since I don't know the first thing about welding, for now, I'm leaving them alone. I may re-visit that decision at a later time.

Hours: 3.5 Manual Ref: Page 9-7 steps 8 & 9 Partner: N/A Just like with final drilling, deburring/dimpling holes in the skins takes a long time.  Here is another time-lapse video showing a good portion of the process.. The wings are going to take forever!
Hours: 3.5 Manual Ref: Page 9-7 steps 8 & 9 Partner: N/A More of the same from a couple days ago. Still more to go!
Hours: 4 Manual Ref: Page 9-7 step 8 Partner: N/A Just a lot of deburring, with a little dimpling.

Hours: 2 Manual Ref: Page 9-7 step 8 Partner: N/A No pictures, just a lot of deburring. I did spend a couple hours on re-assembling the paint booth, but this time in the back yard. Only the time spent deburring is listed in the "2" hours above.

Hours: 5 Manual Ref: Page 9-7 steps 5, 8, and 9; Page 9-16 steps 1 & 4 Partner: N/A Still more dimpling and deburring. Just for a little change in the monotony, I thought I'd try cleco'ing together the trim tabs.

Hours: 5 Manual Ref: Pages 10-2 and 10-3 Partner: N/A In an effort to further push off priming, I've decided to continue on to the tailcone. The first few pages seem to be pretty straight forward at this point. I don't have a tap yet, so I had to skip that part on page 10-2 step 1. Otherwise, everything seemed to work out pretty well.

Hours: 1.5 Manual Ref: Pages 10-4 and 10-5 steps 1 & 2 Partner: N/A It sure is nice putting together large pieces. The sense of accomplishment is very apparent, even though I know there is still lots of work to be done. If the rest of the tailcone goes together as easy, I'll be running out of excuses soon on priming everything!

Hours: 3 Manual Ref: Page 10-5 steps 3 & 4; 10-6; 10-7 steps 1 through 6 Partner: N/A The tailcone is coming together nicely.  I managed to cut the notch in the F-1032-R/L angle without too much difficulty.  Lots of deburring needs to be done, but again, I'm wanting to see things put together.  As you can see in the pictures, I've only match drilled the "right" F-1047F stiffener to the bottom skin.  At first I was thinking it was going to be harder than it actually was.  Even this far into the project, I'm still amazed at how precise everything fits together.  The stiffeners worked out to the exact length they were supposed to be.  I guess I must be measuring appropriately.  The plans stated that the saw horses were to be placed as they are in the picture, no idea why.  The next few steps have the whole assembly placed right side up.  I'm just following the instructions, curious as to how the assembly text changes with the wings and fuselage plans.

Hours: 3 Manual Ref: Page 10-7 step 7; Page 10-8 steps 1, 2, and 3 Partner: N/A The "left" side definitely adds a lot.  I'm starting to get a sense for how big this plane really is.  The stiffeners are certainly time consuming.

Hours: 4 Manual Ref: Page 10-7 step 7; Page 10-8, 10-9 steps 1, 2 & 3; Page 10-10 step 1, 4, 5, & 6; Page 10-12 steps 1, 2, 4, & 7 Partner: N/A It has been a while (a week) since I was last able to work on the project. As I've done a few times now, I skipped a couple steps in the interest of seeing how the various pieces are to go together. As you can see from the pictures below, it is starting to look like I have an airplane!

Hours: 3 Manual Ref: Page 10-11 steps 1, 2; Page 10-13 step 1 Partner: N/A Getting the skins to line up exactly perfect took a bit of effort, but I believe they are pretty darn close.  Drilling through 1/8" of angle aluminum is definitely tougher than the thinner aluminum sheet I've been getting accustom to drilling.  After getting about a 1/3 of the way through the left side, I decided to skip ahead a bit and go back to cutting angle (instead of drilling it).  Again the plans go into some pretty precise detail on the measurements.  Thankfully, this is starting to get easier now.

Hours: 3 Manual Ref: Page 7-9 steps 1 through 8 Partner: Bill Thomasson At $75 a pint (Aircraft Spruce), proseal is some expensive stuff. I had purchased a pint back in December in preparation for glueing the rudder trailing edge. Come to find out, Vans sells the stuff in much smaller quantities. In talking to Bill (a fellow RV-10 builder), we decided to try doing the trailing edge steps at the same time, that way not wasting any more of the proseal than was necessary. I think it worked out pretty good. The stuff is extremely messy, and thankfully I read up on how other builders did theirs. Paper plates and popsicle sticks are the way to go!  Now it is time to wait until the stuff dries and see just how good we did :-). Note: In the pictures below, the pictures of the rudder with the vinyl removed around the rivet locations is mine. The pictures of the inside of the rudder (grey primer) are of Bill's rudder.

Hours: 3 Manual Ref: Page 10-11 step 2 Partner: John Post Just after Bill left, John arrived to see the progress being made. He helped me finish drilling the remaining holes between the bottom side skins and the longerons. We made pretty good progress. It would have taken me a lot longer by myself.

Hours: 3 Manual Ref: Page 7-10 steps 1 through 6 Partner: N/A Since it had been a couple days since Bill and I applied the proseal to the rudder trailing edge, it is now time to start riveting again. It seems strange to be using pop rivets on the spar, but that's the way the plans say to do it. The riveting went pretty easy.

Hours: 4.5 Manual Ref: Page 7-11 steps 1 through 6; Page 7-12 steps 1 through 5 Partner: N/A After having read about all the fuss over curved trailing edges, I spent a great deal of effort ensuring that the edge stayed as straight as possible.  Like several other builders, I also alternated the shop heads of the rivets on each side of the rudder.  The plans also state to back rivet the rivet about 1/2 way, starting vertical then rotating to perpendicular to the skin.  Afterwards I went back with the mushroom set and flatened out the shop heads, so that no part of the rivet protruded proud of the skin.  In the end, the trailing edge is as straight as the best straight edge ruler I have.  It doesn't get much better than that! I also recorded a time-lapse video of this process. Rolling the leading edge proved to be a bit harder than the riveting of the trailing edge.  The short section near the top was easy enough, but that middle section was quite difficult.  Thankfully I've been working out, because the twisting of the broom handle took every bit of strength I had.  Once I got the clecos in, things started getting a little easier.  The next hard part was having to final drill the holes with the #30 bit, then deburring.  Once the skin was bent into a curve, getting the burring tool in there was a challenge.  To finish up, the pop rivets went in with no problems at all. Installing the lead counterbalance weight was quite the interesting process.  There was a lot of "bend the skin this way", and "bend the skin that way" going on.  The plans said to use a #8 screw as the temporary holder of the lead weight to the rib flange.  I opted to use a couple 5/32 clecos.  The only part that I didn't completely understand how to do was the dimpling of the holes put in the skin to hold the weight in place.  The holes are drilled to #19 in size, and I don't have a "#19 dimple die".  I used my 1/8 dimple die set and the machine countersunk holes in the weight to complete the dimple using the head of the #8 screw that holds it all in place.  All in all, it seemed to come out right in the end.  Now I have a completed rudder!

Hours: 1.5 Manual Ref: Page 10-11 steps 3 through 5 Partner: N/A I had a couple hours before trivia, so naturally I spent it final drilling the holes in common to the skins and bulkheads. No pictures, as there isn't anything new to see. Soon, it will be time to add the top skins!

Hours: 6 Manual Ref: Pages 10-12 through 10-14 Partner: John Post I managed to knock out quite a bit today. The top skins were much easier to work with since I had already taken them off and put them back on several times now. The plans say to crimp the flanges with 2 holes. At first, I didn't know if that would help any... it does make the holes in the skins line up a little better with the bulkheads. Also, the stiffeners were much easier to drill. I guess it was because I was drilling down, rather than sideways. The elevator stops and shoulder harness anchors went pretty quickly, as John did the drilling on those.

Hours: 8 Manual Ref: Pages 10-15 step 4 Partner: Karen Michael I spent most of the morning deburring a few of the tailcone parts.  I also spent a little time deburring the horizontal stabilizer skins.  By the time the afternoon had rolled around, my mom came by and helped me re-assemble the paint booth.  Afterwards, there was more deburring to be done!

Hours: 7 Manual Ref: Pages 8-9 step 9 Partner: N/A As Lewis Carroll put it so eloquently, "the time has come, the Walrus said, to talk of many things"!  It should be no surprise that priming is my least favorite (so far) activity of the building process.  But it has to be done.  I do have to say that I like having the paint booth in the back yard much better than in the garage.  The whole process is a lot easier, albeit, time consuming.  7 hours, and all I have to show for it can bee seen in the pictures below.  Granted, there was a lot of prep-work that took place which shouldn't have to be duplicated.

Hours: 10 Manual Ref: Pages 8-9 steps 6 through 9 Partner: Chase Michael It has been a little while since I have posted my progress. Fear not, I have not stopped building. I'm just spending time doing a 100 different things and doing the less exciting work of dimpling and deburring the myriad of pieces in preparation for priming. The time total above is a best guess for all the time put in over the past couple weeks.

For our 2nd annual hike, Roger, Carrie, and I took a trip to south Georgia to see Providence Canyon. The Georgia State Parks website states that the canyon was started due to "poor agricultural processes". I'm sure humans had a hand in starting all of it, but mother nature definitely could have done it all on her own. The soil is quite loose, but not quite sand, so it washes away with water quite readily. Regardless, it is neat to see Georgia's "Grand Canyon". The hiking is pretty easy, too. Don't let the ranger description of "difficult" fool you. This is an easy hike (for the experienced hiker). The elevation change is not more than a couple hundred feet, and most of it is flat. For this trip, we even brought along Carrie's 5 year old son, who had no trouble handling the 10 or so miles of trails.

Hours: 16 Manual Ref: Page 8-9 steps 7, 8 and 9; Page 8-10 Partner: N/A I finally muscled my way through priming the horizontal stabilizer parts, and managed to squeeze a few rivets. Just because it has been awhile since I've done anything with the HS parts, I figured I'd do another test fit. It sure feels good to be finished with all that priming!

Hours: 1 Manual Ref: Page 8-9 step 7 Partner: N/A I thought I'd try dimpling the rib flanges after I primed them this time. It seems to work pretty well. The process of applying the acetone I've been using (a paper towel) goes a whole lot better, as the dimpled holes tend to tear up the paper towel faster. The dimpling doesn't seem to affect the primer too much when done after the fact.

Hours: 1 Manual Ref: Page 8-9 step 8 Partner: N/A I thought I'd try machine counter sinking the spar flanges after I primed them this time. I don't know if I like this as much as dimpling after priming. I think I'll stick to machine countersinking _before_ priming, and dimpling after priming.

Hours: 8 Manual Ref: Page 8-6 step 1; Page 8-10 step 2; Page 8-11 Partner: John Post John is an early riser, so he came by the house about 7:30 and we got right to work. We spent most of the time preparing the last few parts of the HS structure for riveting, then actually riveting together the ribs. Also, now that the spars are all primed, I jumped back a few pages to complete the riveting on page 8-6. Those AN470AD4-9 and AN470AD4-10 rivets are monsters! It took quite a bit of effort even with the 3x gun. John took some pictures of me with his iPhone, but I don't have them yet. I'll have to update this post as soon as I get them.
I'll got to spend some time at Udvar-Hazy on my trip to see my sister.  Definitely worth a visit, if not two ;)

Hours: 0.5 Manual Ref: Page 10-2 step 1 Partner: N/A I again had a few minutes to spare before trivia, and I had just received my tap set in the mail, so I spent about a half-hour tap'ing the rear tie-down. Not too difficult :-)

Hours: 5 Manual Ref: Page 8-13 step 1 Partner: N/A I've ordered a longeron yoke for my squeezer so that I can get at those hard to reach rivets in the forward HS spar. It won't arrive 'till Fri, so in the mean time I decided to rivet the nose ribs to the skins. I seem to have misplaced my soldering iron, so I'm trying a new technique of removing the vinyl from the skins... a pocket knife. So far, I have far fewer scratches, so I think I may keep with this technique. Albeit, it is a LOT slower. Hopefully I'll be making a lot of progress this weekend :-)

Hours: 9 Manual Ref: Page 8-13 step 2, 3, and 4 Partner: N/A In my usual way, I took my time bucking the rivets along the front spar of the horizontal stabilizer.  I think I'm actually getting used to riveting with the rivet gun.  The only problem is... there are a LOT of rivets!  And to think, I'm not even on the wings yet!  There's still more to do, so maybe I'll finish tomorrow afternoon... maybe.  Oh, and I made another time-lapse video for everyone's enjoyment :)

Hours: 5.5 Manual Ref: Page 8-13 steps 3, 4 and 5 Partner: N/A After all the Easter festivities, I managed to spent a few more hours driving rivets. I'm very close to be finished now, as all that is left is squeezing the ones along the flanges of the rear spar and the end ribs.

Hours: 2 Manual Ref: Page 8-13 steps 6 and 7 Partner: N/A Between getting home from work, walking the dog, and going to trivia, I had a couple hours to devote to squeezing a few rivets. Almost there... just a few more clecos to go and I'll have a completed horizontal stabilizer. The rivets along the rear spar are MUCH easier than those along the ribs!

Hours: 2 Manual Ref: Page 8-13 step 7 Partner: John Post Due to some "technical difficulties" at the office, I was not able to spend much time finishing up the rivets on the horizontal stabilizer. However, John dropped by to lend a hand. He squeezed off most of the remaining rivets along the ribs on either end of the HS. He also noticed that my squeezer doesn't keep it's depth setting for very long, so he re-visited all the rivets I had squeezed in the previous few days to ensure they are all properly set. With that done, I was able to complete the remaining few rivets to finally complete chapter 8 of the plans.

Hours: 7 Manual Ref: Page 9-10 step 1 Partner: N/A The time has come yet again to break out the acetone, alumiprep, and primer. Thankfully, I had already primed a bunch of the elevator parts along with the HS. All that remained were the rear spars, skins, and some of the ribs. After all the priming was finished, it was time for my usual final test fit. Everything appears to be in order. Looking forward to riveting some more :)

Hours: 3 Manual Ref: Page 9-10 step 2 Partner: N/A Started the riveting process again. Oddly, getting the rivet squeezer over the flanges was the most challenging part of the process. One thing I've learned about riveting... always secure the work piece.

Hours: 3 Manual Ref: Page 9-10 steps 4, 5, 6 and 7; Page 9-11 steps 1, 2 and 3 Partner: N/A The riveting is going pretty well now.  Cutting out the "foam" ribs was much easier than I thought it was going to be.  The band saw helped tremendously!  The other concern I had, had to do with the nut plates.  I've seen it mentioned that some have cut portions of their dimple die sets to allow for the nut plate holes to be dimpled properly.  I did not bother.  The nut plates appear to have turned out just fine... and I didn't have to alter my dimple die :-)
Hours: 4 Manual Ref: Page 9-11 steps 3 through 6 Partner: N/A I spent a few more hours riveting on the right elevator.  Still have the left one to go...  shouldn't be too long now.
Hours: 4 Manual Ref: Page 9-10 and Page 9-11 steps 1 through 3 Partner: N/A Catching up the left elevator to where I am on the right. It goes very quickly having done all the same steps before.
Hours: 2 Manual Ref: Page 9-11 steps 3 through 6 Partner: N/A Still catching up the left elevator to where I am on the right.

post_title: Now a little of both elevators
post_content: Hours: 6 Manual Ref: Page 9-12 and 9-13 Partner: N/A It was a busy weekend, but I managed to spend a few hours on the elevators.  The plans made it seem like the pulled rivets towards the rear spar (small area in the back of the 2nd and third pictures) would be more challenging than they actually were. Having the special bucking bar for the rear spar made that part very easy.  The rest was just a lot of squeezing.

Hours: 2 Manual Ref: Page 9-15 step 8 and 9-16 step 2 Partner: N/A The lead weights that come with the kit are quite interesting to cut with a band saw. I've never worked with actual lead before. It truly is a "soft" metal. I think I spent as much time cleaning the blade of the band saw as I did cutting the weights. The ribs for the trim tabs went much quicker.

Hours: 4 Manual Ref: Page 9-14 steps 1 through 6 Partner: N/A It took a while, but I managed to get the rivets in on the ends of the left elevator. The right should go much quicker, now that I know how to do it.  Thankfully there is enough room between the end and the next rib to not have to bend the skins too much.  Note to other builders, watch the plans on page 9-20 for the upper skin.  The rivets are different on the upper skin from the bottom one when it comes to where the tip skin gets riveted to the main elevator skin.

post_title: Getting the elevators ready for ProSeal
post_content: Hours: 4 Manual Ref: Page 9-14 steps 1 through 6 Partner: N/A In hopes of having the elevators and trim tabs ready to be "ProSealed" in the next few days, I finished up the last bits for what the plans say to do on page 9-14, before the ProSeal'ing begins.

Hours: 5 Manual Ref: Page 9-16; Page 9-17 steps 1 through 7 Partner: N/A Today was trim tab day. Making the homemade break was quick and easy, and does a very effective job of making sure the bend in the trim tab skin is even. Bending the ends was another story. The plans say to place the wood block 1/32" from the edge of the skin. Even with the double sided tape, my wood block moved upon hitting it with the flush set. Eventually, I got it all straightened out, but it was a lot of work. The 15 degree bend in the lower skin turned out to be fairly simple as well.  My rig to check the angle was a very last minute idea. :-) The rest is just deburring and dimpling and countersinking... routine at this point.

Hours: 4 Manual Ref: Page 10-15 step 4 Partner: N/A With the trim tabs ready for priming, it is time once again to debur. Hopefully I can accumulate a bunch of parts to prime all at once, so I don't have to setup the sprayer too many times. I'm sure there'll be several posts about deburring over the next week or two. ;-)
Hours: 4 Manual Ref: Page 10-15 step 4 Partner: N/A As predicted, more deburring. Not much in the way of new things to see, so no pictures.

Hours: 4 Manual Ref: Page 10-15 step 4 Partner: N/A Still more deburring. Since the process has been an hour here and an hour there, I figured I do a "catchup" post. No pictures, as there still isn't all that much to see.

Hours: 4 Manual Ref: Page 10-15 step 4 Partner: N/A I had a few hours that I could devote to deburring, so I made a bit of progress. The right tailcone skin is now complete and ready for priming. All that is really left is all those small gaps between the flanges of the various bulkheads, the left tailcone skin, half of the bottom tailcone skin, and the back top skin. At the rate I'm going, that should all take through the weekend. After the Thursday night dinner, Randy Epstein and I went up for a hour around lake Lanier and Jackson county's airport in his Piper Warrior. I finally got a chance to see a completed version of what I've been building. Not only did I get to see an RV-10, I actually got to got for a short flight in one! I can safely say, I picked the right plane. Thanks to Bill Thomasson, we took the short flight from KLZU (Gwinnett County) to GA04 (Mallards Landing) to pickup a bag Bill "forgot". This was to be a day of firsts for me, as it was also my first time landing on a grass strip. Naturally, Bill was PIC, but it was still an experience landing on grass. Mallards Landing is such a nice place, I could definitely see myself living there (or somewhere like it) someday. Everyone's got to have a dream, right? Thankfully, Vic was very gratious and invited us over to see his RV, and took us up for a joy ride.  Since this was his 8th (I think) RV, he definitely knows a thing or two about building RVs, and was very helpful with advise on things to do and not do while building. After a quick briefing on safety issues, we were in the plane. Vic mentioned a quote that I like a lot, to show that "Experimental" is a very subjective term. "The Ark was built by Noah, who was an amateur, the Titanic was built by professionals, and it crashed." :-) The RV-10 is quite nice on the inside, and the visibility outside is terrific, as you can see in this video. As for handling, I don't think it will take me long to get used to it. Flying the Zodiac helped a little, but the -10 is soooooo much faster! Bill was a little less timid at the controls and managed to maintain altitude a bit better than me. I just kept wanting to climb (not a good thing under the class B of Atlanta). All in all, the weather was perfect, the plane was perfect, and the experience was something I'll remember for a long time.

For the Georgia Air Challenge, sponsored by the Atlanta Aero Club, ATP and others, I took The Flight School's Zodiac up for a circle route around Atlanta. My plan was as follows: KLZU -> KRYY 2gal 32nm 00:22 ETE KRYY -> KCTJ 2gal 36nm 00:24 ETE KCTJ -> KFFC 2gal 33nm 00:22 ETE Stopping to pick up some items at AircraftSpruce KFFC -> KMLJ 4gal 68nm 00:45 ETE KMLJ -> KLZU 3gal 61nm 00:41 ETE --------------------------------------------------- Total 13gal 230nm 2:35 ETE in-flight Those times were all "in-flight" times, so I expected the trip to take a little longer than that.  The sky over Atlanta was fairly clear, so I managed to get a few pictures. My first stop was Cobb County's McCollum field (KRYY).  I've been to KRYY before, but since it is more than 25nm from LZU, it counts in the challenge.  The landing was un-eventful, but while on the ground, I saw a friend's L-39 taxi'ing to runway 28.  I got a few pictures, and a short video of the takeoff. After KRYY, I was off to West Georgia Regional - Carrollton (a.k.a. KCTJ). The weather was degrading quite a bit, so before I could make it to the field, I chose to divert to my next planned stop, Falcon Field in Peachtree City, GA (a.k.a. KFFC). While there, I took advantage of being close to Aircraft Spruce, and called up the shuttle to visit the store. After KFFC, I don't have any pictures, but the rest of the trip went fairly well. The landing at Milledgeville was a first for me. I'd never landed with an approach over water before. Granted, it was just a lake, but it was still a water approach. Very neat. Here are some screenshots from my iPhone of the trip route and flight plan. In the end, I have 3 takeoffs and landings at airports in Georgia, more than 25nm from KLZU, during the month of July and the trip took 3.2 hours.
