post_title: Denali Day 2 - Arrival at the Park
post_content: After a few hours rest, we get some breakfast in the main lodge. The view off the back porch is meant to be able to see Mt. McKinley, 40 miles away, according to the sign. We weren't too lucky this morning. After another 2 hour drive, we arrive at the Denali National Park entrance and make our way to the backcountry office to figure out what we can do.  We get an extra bear vault, buss passes, food for the hike, and stay overnight in Riley Creek campground.

After a short planning session, we began our hike upstream on Riley Creek through section 1. This was the only trail we traversed in the park.  The trail close to the Riley Creek campground is quite well maintained, complete with bridges and a nice 4 foot wide path.  After getting just south of little creek, we left the trail and started downhill to Riley Creek for our first crossing into section 2. We also crossed little creek so as to stay on the ridge just north of it. Bushwhacking up the ridge was rather challenging but we eventually found a place to camp. Later we'd realize this was the best campsite we'd have the whole trip.

We continue bushwhacking up the mountain until we finally get up to the ridge. Along the way we see a large "glacial erratic" on the ridge to the north, and evidence of local wildlife. We hiked along the ridge for a while and setup camp towards the western side of section 2.

While having breakfast we saw a mother grizzly bear and her 3 cubs descend from the ridge just above us. They were just coming down to get some water and went pack up over the ridge. We were definitely closer than the 1/4 mile the rangers say to stay away from bears. Needless to say, we were a little shaken up. Throughout the day we would see more bears (8 total) and a moose and caribou. The first part of the day's hike was up along the ridge line, but when we crossed into section 4, it was pretty solid bushwhacking down to the savage river. We setup camp just 100 yards off the river bank.

Bushwhacking was the keyword for the day's hike. They say not to follow the animal trails, but I don't know if it would have been possible not to. The willow is really dense in this area. We only had 1 river crossing, the Jenny, and it was pretty close to the savage river campground. It took us so long to bushwhack our way down the river, we missed our bus to section 9. The camp host at savage river was extremely nice and let us stay over night in their teepee. Luxurious accomodations compared to what we'd been staying in. The campground had a program called "tracks and skat" which we attended I made sure to verify with the ranger giving the presentation that the stuff we'd been walking on was in fact tundra.

As we were preparing for our bus ride to section 9, the camp host came over to tell us that Denali (a.k.a. Mt. McKinley) was very clearly visible. And it was, but the snow was too much for my iPhone to handle, so it just looks like a took a picture of a road through some trees. We hopped on a bus and ride the 3 hours to Toklat river. On the way, we passed by the Teklanika river, which means large river, little water in the native Athabascan tongue of the area.   Shortly after passing the Teklanika, we came upon some sheep.  The bus driver put it best when she said "well, I guess we are now on sheep time". After departing the bus, we started our hike south, up the Toklat. The backcountry rules state that we must camp at least 1/2 mile and out of sight of the road. That was quite a challenge as you can see nearly all of section 9 from the road. We did eventually find a spot about 3.5 to 4 miles up the river

Jonathan and Dave wanted to go see one of the glaciers towards the southern end of section 9. My feet were too worn out to make the 18 mile round trip, so I stayed in camp to rest. When I woke up, there were 4 doll sheep resting on the southern face of divide mountain, just to the west of me.

It was a very cold night. We later found out from a ranger that it got down to 28 degrees F overnight. Our hike back to the road didn't take long, and we eventually got on a bus Eielson. Where we switched buses for the rest of the trip out to Kantishna. There were a LOT of tourists from Asia and Australia in the park. It was nice to have some interesting discussions for the 3 hour ride from Toklat to Kantishna. Upon arrival we checked in at the skyline lodge, run by Katair. If you ever get a chance, stay with them and take a scenic air tour up to see Denali. Katair had some seats available on a couple scenic flights around the mountain in the evening, and we agreed to go. It was quite an experience. Our pilots were Andy and Connie, and both truly know their stuff. Needless to say, I got a few pictures and videos (4:17 min 2:45min 5:00 min 1:32 min). Later in the evening, after Dave and the owner Greg, had a mini ping-pong match, we found out that the Aurora was visible the night before. So Dave and I stayed up until about 1 AM in an attempt to see it. No joy :(

With only a few hours sleep, we got up, had breakfast, and hopped in the plane for the trip back to the park entrance. This time all of us were in the plane with Connie. He was quite entertaining, and managed to get us some time around Denali on the way back. Also, on the way back, we over-flew the range (3:29 min) that we had been hiking on earlier in the trip. Boy would it have been nice to have flown over it in the first place :). The landing at the park entrance was uneventful, but neat. It was my first landing on a "gravel" runway (2:49 min). Our car was literally on the other side of the railroad tracks from the landing strip, so we didn't have far to walk with our packs. That was nice. After a little repacking for the flight home from Anchorage, we got some lunch and started the 5 hour drive back to Anchorage. On the drive, we tried to figure out what there was to do in Anchorage for the 8 or so hours that we would be there. Turns out, there isn't all that much to do in Anchorage. We did a little walking around town and got dinner at a local pizza cafe. We all had the same flight from Anchorage to Phoenix. Then we split up, Dave and Jonathan heading to Boston, and I went to Atlanta. All in all about 36 hours of travel time, with about 15 hours of actual "moving" time.

post_title: Sealing up the fuel tanks - part 1
post_content: Hours: 8 Manual Ref: Page 18-5 steps 8, 10 and 11 Partner: Bill Thomason Well, the time has come to bite the bullet and start sealing and riveting together the fuel tanks. All-in-all, the process went far better than I was expecting, although my expectations were probably fairly negative.  Having Bill's assistance helped tremendously, especially when placing the ribs into the skins.  Proseal, or ChemSeal in my case, is VERY sticky stuff, but it somehow seemed to make the ribs "slip" into place a lot better than when I was fitting pieces together for final drilling. I didn't have all the parts ready to complete the steps in plans order, but after reviewing the entire riveting process, the 3 steps we did work on looked like they could be done first.  The first parts to get done were the stiffeners, and they were back riveted.  After those were all in place, the ribs were installed.  To make things go a little quicker, we just cleco'ed the ribs in place, rather than rivet each as it was installed.  Then we added the J-channel.  The plans say to put the sealant on the skin, rather than the J-channel, but it just seemed easier to us to put it on the J-channel directly, then slide the J-channel in place.  Having done it once, successfully, I'd do it the same way again. After Bill left, I finished riveting all the parts that were just cleco'ed on.  So far, so good.  That's a large portion of the right fuel tank done.  Now to get the left tank up to speed :-)

About once a year, the EAA comes to Lawrenceville to provide a few classes in airplane construction. They call these classes the "EAA SportAir Workshops". I took the "Sheet Metal Basics" course last year, just before I ordered the empennage. This year, I figured the best class to take was the "Electrical Systems & Avionics" course. The big change this year was that the classes were not being held at KLZU, rather they were at the Aviation Institute of Maintenance... which moved from KLZU about a year or so ago. Their new facility is actually quite nice. While waiting for registration to begin, I took a few pictures of the various equipment and projects that were being worked on. The avionics class itself was held in a classroom down the hall, but more suited to the material that we would be going over. The highlights of the class were of course the hands on projects. The first of which was attaching ends to wires. The "crimping exercise" consisted of two 6" wires (AWG 18), a ring connector, a butt connector, and a molex connector. The goal is perform an example of the connectors common for most power and avionics systems. The next project was a typical headset harness. This one required the use of soldering, shrink tubing, and being able to read a wiring diagram. After everything was assembled, we got to see if we did it right by hooking up the harness to an actual headset (and a tester). I was pleased to have mine work on the first try :-) Day 2, since daylight savings time was over (too bad not permanently), I got to class a little early and took some pictures of the various pieces of equipment used for demonstration purposes in the class. Stuff only an electronics geek could love. After a couple more hours of lecture, it was time for the 3rd exercise. This time it was a BNC crimping exercise. We were handed a piece of RG-58 and a BNC connector. The key to this exercise was getting the lengths of each layer of the wire correct. In the end, not all that hard to do. After lunch, there was time for just a few more tips and tricks, and then we were off onto our last exercise. The panel wiring exercise is designed to use most of what is learned in the entire course. It includes a battery, power and ground bus, light bulbs for each circuit, a switch, fuse, and a dimmer. All of the rest of the work (like building the aluminum box) was done for us. All-in-all, I'd say the class is definitely worth the time and money, as I certainly learned a lot, and was made aware of some items that I might include in my plane when it comes time to add the electrical system to it.

As I posted on Facebook "Lucky me woke up today to find the toilet overflowing :(". Apparently there is something wrong with the downstairs toilet. Looks like I'll not be getting around to the things I was planning on doing this weekend.

After a bit of diagnosing, it turns out the real problem was roots in the septic tank. The story goes as follows: After spending a few hours pulling up carpet and throwing soaked padding into the backyard, a friend came over to help try to figure out what was wrong. The result was a call to Roto-Rooter. The Roto-Rooter guy came out, took a quick look at the problem and asked "when was the last time you had your septic tank pumped?". It was eerie that some neighbors of mine had been talking recently about having their septic tank pumped. In the interest of not paying $450 to Roto-Rooter to _maybe_ fix the problem, I contacted Aames Plumbing to have the tank pumped. The guy from Aames (Nick), opened up the tank and pretty quickly determined the problem was roots. So my $300 tank pumping turned into a $1300 pumping and de-rooting project. Thankfully, all is now well with the septic system... now on to fixing the house!
